## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sādhusīlajātaka* (Ja 200), translated in modern listings as "Good is Virtue," is a canonical Jātaka tale belonging to the *Jātaka* collection of the Pali Tipiṭaka [SuttaCentral]. In the Pali text and commentary edited by V. Fausböll, it constitutes the tenth and final story of the *Ruhakavagga*, the fifth section of the *Dukanipāta* [Fausböll 1879]. The story is framed by a setting at Jetavana, where the Buddha addresses a situation involving a certain brahmin with four daughters [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. Four suitors sought the daughters in marriage: one was handsome and well-formed (*abhirūpo sarīrasampanno*), one elderly (*vayappatto mahallako*), one of noble birth (*jātisampanno*), and one virtuous (*sīlavā*) [Fausböll 1879]. Resolving to bestow the daughters upon the virtuous man, the brahmin followed the advice of a world-renowned teacher (*disāpāmokkhācariya*), whom the Buddha identifies in the *samodhāna* as having been himself in a past life [Fausböll 1879].

Textual reuse analysis by DharmaNexus identifies four matching segments between the verses of the *Sādhusīlajātaka* and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), the longest span encompassing segments §2.1–2.4 aligned with commentary sections §847–848 at a 0.95 similarity score [DharmaNexus]. Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies any cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan traditions [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations across four languages [SuttaCentral].
